Master the Pokémon type chart with our complete guide. Learn all 18 types, their strengths, weaknesses, immunities, and how to build teams with optimal type coverage.

The Pokémon type chart is the foundation of all battles. Understanding type effectiveness — which types are strong against which, and which are weak — is essential for success in both casual and competitive play. This guide covers all 18 types, their matchups, and strategies for using them effectively.

Table of Contents

  1. The 18 Pokémon Types
  2. Type Effectiveness Explained
  3. Complete Type Chart
  4. Dual-Type Matchups
  5. Generation Changes
  6. Type Strategies
  7. Conclusion

The 18 Pokémon Types

The Pokémon franchise features 18 different types: Normal, Fire, Water, Grass, Electric, Ice, Fighting, Poison, Ground, Flying, Psychic, Bug, Rock, Ghost, Dragon, Dark, Steel, and Fairy. Each type has specific strengths and weaknesses against other types, creating a complex web of interactions that defines the battle system.

Each type also has its own theme and characteristics. Fire types are associated with heat and flames, and are typically offensively oriented. Water types are versatile and defensive, with a wide movepool. Grass types are associated with nature and have unique status moves. Electric types are fast and hit hard with Electric moves.

Understanding the thematic and mechanical differences between types helps you predict opponent moves and build better teams. Let us explore each type in detail and examine their strengths and weaknesses.

Type Effectiveness Explained

In Pokémon battles, type effectiveness determines how much damage a move deals. A super effective move deals double damage, while a not very effective move deals half damage. Some type combinations are completely immune to certain types, dealing zero damage.

For example, a Fire-type move against a Grass-type Pokémon is super effective and deals double damage. A Water-type move against a Water-type Pokémon is not very effective and deals half damage. A Normal-type move against a Ghost-type Pokémon has no effect and deals zero damage.

Dual-type Pokémon can have complex effectiveness patterns. If both types are weak to the move, it deals quadruple damage. If both types resist the move, it deals quarter damage. If one type is immune, the move has no effect regardless of the other type.

Dual-Type Matchups

Dual-type Pokémon have complex effectiveness patterns that combine the strengths and weaknesses of both types. This can create interesting interactions, such as a Pokémon that takes quadruple damage from one type but is immune to another.

For example, a Water/Ground type like Swampert is immune to Electric and takes only quarter damage from Poison, but takes quadruple damage from Grass. A Steel/Fairy type like Mawile has 9 resistances, 2 immunities, and only 2 weaknesses (Fire and Ground).

When building a team, look for dual types that cover each other weaknesses. A Fire/Water/Grass core is a classic example, as each type resists the others weaknesses. Other good cores include Steel/Fairy/Dragon and Fire/Steel/Fairy.

Generation Changes

The type chart has evolved over the generations. In Generation 1, Ghost-type moves had no effect on Psychic types, which was a bug that was fixed in Generation 2. Generation 2 introduced the Dark and Steel types to balance the overpowered Psychic type.

Generation 6 introduced the Fairy type to balance the overpowered Dragon type. Fairy is strong against Dragon, Dark, and Fighting, and is weak to Fire, Poison, and Steel. This addition significantly changed the competitive landscape, making Poison and Steel types more valuable offensively.

Generation 9 introduced Terastallize, which allows Pokémon to change their type temporarily. This adds a new layer of strategy to type matchups, as a Pokémon can Terastallize to gain resistances or offensive advantages that were not available before.

Type Strategies

Understanding the type chart is just the beginning. To be successful in battles, you need to apply this knowledge strategically. Here are some key strategies:

  • Cover your weaknesses: Build a team where each member covers the weaknesses of others.
  • Use STAB moves: Same Type Attack Bonus moves deal 1.5x damage, making them your primary offensive option.
  • Predict switches: If you expect your opponent to switch, use a move that hits the incoming Pokémon.
  • Use entry hazards: Stealth Rock and Spikes wear down opponents based on their typing.
  • Consider abilities: Abilities like Levitate, Flash Fire, and Water Absorb can change type matchups.
  • Use Terastallize wisely: In Generation 9, Terastallize can change your type to gain defensive or offensive advantages.

Conclusion

The Pokémon type chart is the foundation of all battles. By understanding type effectiveness, dual-type matchups, and type strategies, you can build teams that succeed in any format. Whether you are a casual player or a competitive battler, mastering the type chart is essential.
